# Just Once

> "Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that plunder the vineyards; for our vineyards are in blossom."
>
> — Song of Solomon 2:15

"Just once" is a myth. Get it out of your head.

- Just once is how every one of us began.
- Just once, to get through a rough week or to mark a special occasion, is what has sunk most of your attempts to stop.
- Just once is what puts a man back in the trap after he's been free for months. Sometimes he does it only to prove he doesn't need it anymore, and it proves the opposite.

Men say afterward that the habit "came back". It didn't come back by itself. It was let in, once.

What follows "just once" is always the same. The flatness lands, and it's so grim that the man is certain nothing this miserable could ever hook him again.

But it already has.

Within a day or two the pull for another one arrives. Men call it the chaser. The Little Monster is awake and fed. The man sits there baffled that a thing which makes him feel this bad could have made him do it. Yet it did.

## The special one {-}

You know the voice that sells it. It says it's just one more time, just one more video, and you can get back to your purpose after. It always sounds that reasonable, and it always promises that you can go straight back to being the man you meant to be.

It's the thought of one special time that stops many men from ever stopping. The one after a week away on business. The one after the fight. The one on the night she turns over and says she's tired. The one video. The one message to her, "just to say hello". The one you've "earned".

Get this fixed in your mind: JUST ONCE DOES NOT EXIST. It's a chain, and each link is forged by the one before. The myth of the rare special occasion is also what keeps men moping after they've quit. They are like a man who has moved to a new house and keeps driving past the old one.

So train yourself never to picture the single, harmless time. It's a fantasy in every sense. When lust comes to mind, see the whole of it. See thousands of locked doors and thousands of flat ten minutes afterward. See a secret carried through every room you walk into, and the years of your strength poured down a drain. A weak moment isn't a crime. But why choose a lifetime of that, when you could be free?

Don't fool yourself. You can do this. Any man can. It's absurdly easy, so long as you have three things straight:

1. There is nothing to give up. There is only a great deal to gain.
2. Never talk yourself into a harmless "no big deal". It doesn't exist. There is only the whole chain or none of it.
3. There is nothing different about you. Any man can find it easy to stop.

## "I'm just built this way" {-}

Plenty of men believe they're a special case. "I've got an unusually high drive." "I've got an addictive personality." Christians have their own version: "This is my besetting sin, my thorn. I'll carry it to the grave." He is borrowing from Paul, who wrote of a "thorn in the flesh". But Paul's thorn was a suffering God allowed. It was never a sin he was told to keep. Usually the man has picked this up from too many failed streaks and too many alarming videos.

Nobody is born needing to do this to get to sleep. You weren't lying in your crib plotting it. It's the trap that catches a man. His character has nothing to do with it. But the trap is clever enough to make him blame his character. You must drop that belief. A man who believes he's a lifer will behave like one long after the Little Monster is dead.

This chapter opened with a line from the Song of Solomon, a love poem in the Bible: "Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that plunder the vineyards". It doesn't warn about wolves. It warns about little foxes. Nobody loses a vineyard to a wolf. The damage is done by something small enough to slip under the fence while the vines are in flower.

"Just once" is the little fox.
